notes.meaning: This record begins the family history of Aaron and Moses at the time God gave His laws on Mount Sinai. Aaron is named first because his sons inherited the sacred priesthood, while Moses passed down no special office to his own children. At Mount Sinai, Aaron's family was still whole, before two of his sons died.

Aaron had four sons: Nadab the firstborn, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. All four were anointed with holy oil and set apart to serve as priests. During their ordination, Moses placed sacrificial portions into their hands to show they were fully dedicated to the altar service.

Nadab and Abihu died before the Lord when they brought unauthorized fire into the sanctuary instead of fire from the holy altar. Because they died childless, only Eleazar and Ithamar carried on the priesthood under their father Aaron. This severe judgment showed Israel that God's instructions for worship must be obeyed exactly.

The Lord told Moses to bring forward the rest of the tribe of Levi and present them to Aaron the priest. The word used for presenting them was a sacrificial term, showing that the Levites were given to God as a living offering. They were no longer free for ordinary work but were dedicated to assisting the priests.

The Levites had a threefold duty to assist Aaron, help the congregation, and care for the tabernacle. They stood guard around the sanctuary and looked after all its tents and sacred furnishings. By doing the heavy physical labor of setting up and moving the tabernacle, they fulfilled duties owed by the whole nation.

Moses was told to assign the Levites completely to Aaron and his sons to aid them in sanctuary duties. Aaron's family alone held the priestly office of offering sacrifices, and any unauthorized outsider who attempted priestly work was to be put to death. This strict rule guarded the holiness of God's presence among them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars believe the strict division between Aaron's priestly family and the rest of the Levites developed much later in Israel's history rather than at Mount Sinai.

notes.meaning: The Lord declared that He was claiming the tribe of Levi as His own in place of every firstborn male in Israel. During the first Passover in Egypt, God spared Israel's firstborn when Egypt's died, making them His special possession by redemption. Instead of taking the oldest son from every family, God took the whole tribe of Levi as their substitutes.

God commanded Moses to count every male Levite from one month of age and older. Other tribes were counted for warfare starting at age twenty, but Levites were counted from babyhood because they served as substitutes for Israel's firstborn sons. Moses obeyed the Lord completely and registered them family by family.

Levi had three sons named Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, who originally went down into Egypt. These three brothers became the ancestors of the three primary divisions of the Levitical tribe. Every Levite belonged to one of these three branches.

These verses name the grandsons of Levi who founded the individual family clans. Gershon had Libni and Shimei; Kohath had Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel; and Merari had Mahli and Mushi. These eight clans formed the organized groups responsible for the care of the sanctuary.

The first division, descended from Gershon, consisted of the Libnite and Shimeite clans. When Moses counted all the Gershonite males from one month old and older, they totaled 7,500. This made them the middle-sized group among the three Levitical divisions.

The Gershonite clans were assigned to pitch their tents on the west side, right behind the tabernacle. Their chosen leader was Eliasaph, the son of Lael. Their position placed them between the sanctuary and the western camp of Ephraim.

The Gershonites were given charge over all the fabric and leather parts of the sanctuary. Their responsibility included the inner linen tabernacle, the outer goat-hair tent, the protective animal skin coverings, and the screen at the tent entrance. They also took care of the courtyard curtains, the courtyard entrance screen, and the ropes used for the tabernacle structure.
